prompt: Which IEEE amendment does the name Wi-Fi 6 stand for?

choices.text: Whichever standard uses the 6 GHz band
choices.why: The number is a generation, not a band. 6 GHz came with Wi-Fi 6E, which is the same 802.11ax.
That is Wi-Fi 5, the amendment that reached 160 MHz on 5 GHz.

choices.text: 802.11ax, in 2.4 and 5 GHz
choices.why: Right. Wi-Fi 4, 5 and 6 are 802.11n, ac and ax, and the E of 6E adds the third band.

choices.text: 802.11be, the newest amendment
choices.why: 802.11be is Wi-Fi 7.

prompt: A router sold as Wi-Fi 6, with no 6E anywhere on the box, is paired with a Wi-Fi 6E phone. Where does the phone connect?
hint: Which radios does the router have?

choices.text: On 6 GHz, because the phone supports it
choices.why: Both ends need a 6 GHz radio, and this router has none.

choices.text: On 2.4 or 5 GHz, the router's only bands
choices.why: Right. The phone falls back to the bands they share, and its 6 GHz radio stays idle.

choices.text: Nowhere: a 6E phone refuses a plain Wi-Fi 6 network
choices.why: Within a band the standards are backwards compatible.

choices.text: On 6 GHz after a firmware update to the router
choices.why: A band is a radio in the hardware; software cannot add one.

prompt: Match each IEEE amendment to the name the Wi-Fi Alliance gave it.
Put these amendments in the order they were published, oldest first.
trap: 802.11g (2003) came after 802.11b (1999), and ac (2013) after n (2009): the letters were handed out as projects started, not as they finished.

prompt: An 802.11ax access point on 2.4 GHz has one 802.11b client joined, sending a lot. What does it cost the other clients?
hint: What is shared on one channel?

choices.text: Nothing, since each client is served at its own rate
choices.why: Each is served at its own rate, and they share one channel's time: the slow frames occupy it for longer.

choices.text: The other clients drop to 11 Mbit/s
choices.why: The others keep their own rates. What they lose is time on the air, not their modulation.

choices.text: Airtime: its slow frames hold the channel longer
choices.why: Right. The same bytes at 11 Mbit/s occupy the air many times longer than at a modern rate, and everybody else waits.

choices.text: Nothing, because the access point refuses 802.11b
choices.why: Inside a band the standards are backwards compatible; the old client is accepted unless somebody switches its rates off.

prompt: At the same transmit power, why does a 2.4 GHz signal reach further than a 5 GHz one?
hint: It is about the frequency itself.

choices.text: Lower frequencies lose less on the way
choices.why: Right. About 6 dB less in open air, and more again through walls.

choices.text: Regulators allow more power at 2.4 GHz
choices.why: The comparison was at the same power; the difference is in the band.

choices.text: 5 GHz packs more bits into each subcarrier
choices.why: The same modulations exist in both bands.

choices.text: 2.4 GHz has fewer networks competing
choices.why: It is the most crowded band of the three.

prompt: Where all 1200 MHz of the 6 GHz band is open, how many 20 MHz channels that do not overlap does it hold?
A laptop moved from 2.4 GHz to 5 GHz downloads faster. A colleague says 5 GHz is a faster band. What actually changed?
hint: The rate arithmetic has no frequency in it.

choices.text: A shorter wavelength carries more bits per second
choices.why: The rate comes from subcarriers, bits and symbol time, and none of them depends on the band.

choices.text: A wider, less crowded channel
choices.why: Right. 5 GHz has room for wide channels and fewer neighbours; the same channel on 2.4 GHz would run at the same rate.

choices.text: 5 GHz is full duplex and 2.4 GHz is not
choices.why: Every Wi-Fi channel is half duplex, whatever the band.

choices.text: Nothing, the difference is in the laptop's display
choices.why: The download really was faster; the reason is the channel, not the band's name.

prompt: Which of these make the 6 GHz band quieter than 5 GHz? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who is allowed in, and what is not there.

choices.text: Only Wi-Fi 6E and 7 devices can join it
choices.why: Right: no old client to fall back for.

choices.text: There is room for seven 160 MHz channels
choices.why: Right: wide channels without stepping on each other.

choices.text: Indoor low-power access points need no radar detection there
choices.why: Right, unlike a large part of 5 GHz.

choices.text: It passes through walls better than 5 GHz
choices.why: The reverse: it reaches the least of the three, which helps only because next door's signal is weaker too.

prompt: Which channels an access point will offer is decided by the ___ it has been told it is in, not by its hardware.
What does doubling a channel's width buy?

choices.text: A longer reach
choices.why: The reverse: the noise doubles and the signal does not, so the edge of the cell gets worse.

choices.text: More channels to choose from
choices.why: Every doubling halves the number of channels in the band.

choices.text: More subcarriers in each symbol, so a little over twice the rate
choices.why: Right: 286.8 to 600.5 Mbit/s from 40 to 80 MHz, for one 802.11ax stream.

choices.text: Protection from a neighbour on the same frequencies
choices.why: A wider channel overlaps more neighbours, not fewer.

prompt: One 802.11ax stream on 80 MHz at the top modulation runs at 600.5 Mbit/s. What link rate does a phone with two streams get on that channel, in Mbit/s?
Why is 20 MHz the width chosen on 2.4 GHz almost everywhere?

choices.text: 802.11n forbids 40 MHz channels at 2.4 GHz
choices.why: 802.11n allows them. They are a bad idea there, not an illegal one.

choices.text: One 40 MHz channel takes nearly half the band
choices.why: Right. With 83.5 MHz in all, a 40 MHz channel leaves the neighbours nowhere to go.

choices.text: 2.4 GHz clients fail to decode wide channels
choices.why: Any 802.11n client can; the problem is the room, not the clients.

choices.text: Wider channels would run slower at 2.4 GHz
choices.why: The rate would roughly double, as in any band; the cost is to everybody else.

prompt: At the far edge of a cell, a client on a 160 MHz channel gets a lower link rate than it did on 40 MHz. Why?

choices.text: 160 MHz channels are only allowed at lower power
choices.why: The limit is not a rule about power; it is the noise the wider receiver hears.

choices.text: The access point splits its time between four 40 MHz parts
choices.why: It transmits across the whole 160 MHz at once.

choices.text: 6 dB less signal-to-noise, so a slower modulation
choices.why: Right. 3 dB per doubling, twice. At the edge that costs more than the extra subcarriers buy.

choices.text: Only 802.11be clients can use 160 MHz
choices.why: 160 MHz has existed since 802.11ac; 802.11be added 320.

prompt: A 4x4:4 access point talks to a 2x2:2 phone. How many spatial streams does their link carry?

choices.text: Four, the access point's number
choices.why: The phone cannot pull apart more streams than it has antennas to receive.

choices.text: Two
choices.why: Right. The other two are idle for this phone, or used for somebody else with MU-MIMO.

choices.text: Eight, four times two
choices.why: Streams are not multiplied across the two ends.

choices.text: Three, the average of both ends
choices.why: There is no averaging: the link carries what both ends support.

prompt: What does OFDMA in 802.11ax improve most?
hint: Think of a room full of phones sending small packets.

choices.text: One client's top download rate
choices.why: A client alone gets the whole channel either way.

choices.text: The number of streams a phone can receive
choices.why: That is antennas and MIMO, a separate thing.

choices.text: The encryption between each client and the access point
choices.why: OFDMA divides subcarriers; encryption is lesson 8's subject.

choices.text: The cost of many small transmissions
choices.why: Right. Several clients share one transmission, and the cost of winning the air is paid once.

prompt: An office buys MU-MIMO access points, and people there walk about with their phones all day. Why does it gain little?
hint: What does the access point have to know before it aims?

choices.text: MU-MIMO works only in the 6 GHz band, which the phones lack
choices.why: It arrived with 802.11ac, a 5 GHz amendment, and works there.

choices.text: Its path changes before the measurement is used
choices.why: Right. Aiming needs a fresh measurement of each client's path, and a walking phone makes it stale.

choices.text: Phones have a single antenna
choices.why: Phones sold today have two, and one would still be enough to receive one stream.

choices.text: MU-MIMO is for uploads, not downloads
choices.why: 802.11ac's MU-MIMO was downstream only; 802.11ax added upstream.

prompt: An AX1800 router has two streams on a 40 MHz channel at 2.4 GHz (573.6 Mbit/s) and two streams on 80 MHz at 5 GHz (1201 Mbit/s). What is the highest link rate one client can have, in Mbit/s?
hint: A client uses one radio at a time.

prompt: One phone right next to the access point shows a link rate of 1201 Mbit/s and downloads at about 700. Nothing is faulty. What explains most of the gap?

choices.text: Taking turns, and each transmission's fixed costs
choices.why: Right: half duplex, preambles, gaps, random waits and acknowledgements.

choices.text: Encryption, which halves the rate
choices.why: Encryption adds a few bytes per frame, nothing like 40%.

choices.text: The phone rounds the number it displays
choices.why: 1201 is the real link rate; rounding would not remove 500 Mbit/s.

choices.text: The access point caps each client at 60% of the link rate
choices.why: No cap: the 60% of this section is an assumption about overheads, not a setting.

prompt: An office's Wi-Fi is slow all afternoon. The one busy device is an old 802.11g scanner uploading large files. Which change helps the others most?
hint: What does the scanner use up?

choices.text: Widen the channel to 80 MHz
choices.why: 802.11g uses 20 MHz whatever the channel is set to, so its frames take just as long.

choices.text: Raise the access point's transmit power
choices.why: Its best is 54 Mbit/s however loud the access point is.

choices.text: Give the scanner a cable, or replace it
choices.why: Right. Its slow frames were holding the channel; off the air, that time goes back to everybody.

choices.text: Buy an access point with more streams
choices.why: 802.11g has one stream; the new streams would serve everybody but the device using the time.

prompt: Why does this lesson show no capture at all?

choices.text: Wi-Fi frames are encrypted, so a capture shows nothing
choices.why: Encryption hides the payload, not the frames; the lab simply has no frames to capture.

choices.text: The lab has no radio
choices.why: Right. Its machines are joined by virtual Ethernet: full duplex, no noise and no airtime to share, so nothing here would be true of Wi-Fi.

choices.text: tcpdump has no decoder for 802.11
choices.why: It can, given a wireless card to capture from.

choices.text: Capturing radio traffic is against the law
choices.why: Capturing your own network for diagnosis is routine; the lab just has no radio.

prompt: 802.11ax serves several clients in one transmission by giving each its own resource unit of subcarriers, which is called ___.
hint: The change 802.11ax is best known for.

prompt: A café's Wi-Fi 6 access point runs 160 MHz on 5 GHz, beside two neighbours' networks on the same frequencies. Customers at the far tables get slow service. What is the better setting?

choices.text: Move to 2.4 GHz at 40 MHz for the reach
choices.why: The most crowded band, at a width that fills half of it.

choices.text: Stay on 5 GHz at 40 MHz, clear of the neighbours
choices.why: Right. 6 dB better signal-to-noise at the far tables, and a channel nobody else is using.

choices.text: Keep 160 MHz and add a second access point on it
choices.why: Two access points on one channel take turns; the overlap with the neighbours stays.

choices.text: Go to 320 MHz to finish each transfer sooner
choices.why: 802.11ax has no 320 MHz, and wider would make the edge worse.
